analysis.title: EcoWeek 26.42: The global economy's resilience to shocks: Four observations and three intertwined questions
key_insights: The global economy is absorbing the energy shock from the Middle East conflict (outbreak late February) better than the 2022 shock. Brent crossed USD 100 again in October, but PMI/ISM indices stay above 50, clearly so in the US and slightly less so in Europe.

Growth rests on the global investment cycle (AI, military spending, decarbonization and electrification, German infrastructure plan), but household consumption still contributes. US consumption was the largest contributor to growth until Q2 2026 and was overtaken by AI-related investment in Q3 on current data.

Eurozone household consumption grew 0.34% a quarter on average from Q1 2023 to Q2 2026, against 0.66% in the US. It is still the dominant Eurozone growth driver (0.2pp, or 71%, against about half a percentage point for total investment), and the savings rate has not fallen, so there is more room for improvement.

Inflation is mostly energy-driven but looks more entrenched in the US. Eurozone HICP was 4.0% y/y in October with core at 2.6% y/y, and energy is nearly half of the rise. US CPI was 3.7% y/y in September, with core picking up again and nearly 60% of CPI components rising more than 3% (43% in the Eurozone).

10-year sovereign yields near 5% in the US, UK and France are at 25-year highs and bring debt service back as a constraint. The gap between the implicit interest rate on debt and nominal GDP growth is set to reverse by the end of the decade in most European economies, and the interest burden is forecast to double by 2032 in France, Germany and Japan and reach 5% of GDP in the US.

BNP calls the fiscal strain manageable in the short and medium term because of long average debt maturities (Eurozone, Japan, UK) and gradual fiscal consolidation in most European countries (not Germany). The US has no stated consolidation commitment and a shorter average maturity, so rate rises pass through to debt service faster.

BNP's forecasts say the bulk of the rise in long-term yields is behind us, since yields already price resilient growth and residual monetary tightening. Yields could fall later if fiscal consolidation gains credibility.
Recent tech-sector turbulence shows the trade-off. Safe-haven bond buying reduces pressure on long-term rates but raises the downside risk to activity from a reversal of the AI boom.
BNP supports the measured approach of the Fed and ECB and expects further policy rate hikes, but a few rather than many, to fine-tune and extend the growth cycle.

US October CPI surprised to the upside: headline +0.4% m/m, core +0.3% for a third straight month. Waller said a 50bp hike should be considered if core came in hot, and Logan said the FOMC might need to move faster this winter. The 2-year yield rose more than 30bp on the week to 4.85% on 12 November.

Eurozone Q3 GDP was confirmed at +0.4% q/q but employment was flat for the first time since Covid. A package deal on ECB leadership (Hernandez de Cos as President) could be agreed when EU Leaders meet on 18 November.

Japan Q3 GDP was flat q/q, below the 0.1% consensus, and the BoJ October meeting summary shows policymakers no longer see a need to be overly cautious about hikes, signaling a December hike. PPI inflation accelerated to 7.1% y/y in October.

China shows weak domestic demand and booming exports. October exports rose 35.2% y/y in USD, integrated-circuit exports rose 137.1% (mostly price effects), and retail sales rose only 0.4% y/y nominal. CPI was 0.7% y/y and PPI 5.7%.
India CPI rose to 6.1% y/y in October, above the RBI's 6% ceiling for the first time in two years. Another 25bp hike is expected in December after the policy rate was raised to 5.5% in October.

Paraguay's Ueno Bank went into resolution on 2 November. The collapse caused a political crisis and the removal of President Pena, and Fitch put the BB+ rating on Negative Watch on 11 November. BNP does not expect a systemic banking crisis.

Brent rose 3.4% on the week to USD96/bbl after briefly dipping below USD90 on hopes for Iran-US talks. The IEA says October crude supply exceeded demand for the first time since the war began. European gas rose 8% to EUR89/MWh on Gulf LNG constraints, cold weather and Norwegian outages.

risk_factors: Reversal of the AI investment boom, which would hit growth even as it lowers long-term yields.
Further tightening of financial conditions and bank credit access beyond the contained level BNP assumes.
Entrenched US inflation, with producer-price pass-through to consumer prices and core CPI re-accelerating.
Long-term yields near 5% raising debt service costs, with the US most exposed because of shorter average debt maturity and no stated consolidation commitment.
Political uncertainty around fiscal consolidation paths in Europe.
Renewed energy price pressure from Gulf export constraints, European gas supply issues and Middle East escalation.
El Nino-driven food price inflation in Latin America.
Paraguay fiscal and political instability after the Ueno Bank collapse.
Weak Chinese domestic demand and margin compression for consumer-facing firms.
charts_described: Chart shows personal consumption expenditures and AI-related investment as contributions to annual real GDP growth from Q1-2023 to Q3-2026, titled 'AI-related investment rivals the US consumer as the key US growth engine'. Per the text, consumption was the largest contributor until Q2 2026 and AI-related investment overtook it in Q3.
vol_and_positioning: Non-resident portfolio investment flows into emerging markets have been highly volatile since the conflict began, but financing conditions have held up.
Recent turbulence in the tech sector pushed investors toward safe-haven bonds, which lowered long-term rate pressure while raising the downside risk from a reversal of the AI boom.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict that began in late February, including the Iran war, drove the energy shock. Hopes for Iran-US talks briefly pushed Brent below USD90.
Limited Gulf exports of diesel and LNG, and damage to Russian refineries, keep diesel cracks and European gas elevated.
A trilateral summit between Putin, Trump and Xi on the sidelines of the APEC Summit is scheduled for Thursday.
EU Leaders meet on 18 November and may agree a package of ECB leadership appointments.
Paraguay's political crisis after the Ueno Bank collapse led to President Pena's removal.
US midterm politics: cost of living is cited as a pivotal issue in a prior EcoWeek.

tension_points.bull_case: Rising long-term yields reflect resilient growth, the AI boom and risk appetite, and the rise is broadly warranted and orderly. With equities rallying, overall financial conditions are not particularly tightened, and BNP expects the bulk of the rise to be behind us.
tension_points.bear_case: Recent data show first signs of tighter monetary and financial conditions including bank credit. Higher yields strain public finances, and a reversal of the AI boom would hit activity even as safe-haven bond demand lowers yields.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A reversal of the AI boom, or tightening of financial conditions and credit access beyond the contained level BNP assumes, which is its most likely scenario at present.

theme_stances.key_argument: The global economy is weathering the energy shock better than in 2022, with PMI/ISM above 50 and emerging economies resilient.
theme_stances.evidence: the global economy continues to show resilience in the face of the energy shock

theme_stances.key_argument: Further policy rate hikes are expected but a few rather than a lot, to support the growth cycle as long as possible.
theme_stances.evidence: Further hikes in policy rates are to be expected, but rather a few ones than a lot

theme_stances.key_argument: US inflation is more entrenched than the Eurozone's, with core picking up and broad price pressure across the CPI basket.
